Discussing Solutions and Strategies

Have students share the areas they found for the various samples in the Initial Challenge. Compare the findings.

Focus the summary discussion on the strategies used to find the area of the circles.

Making the Mathematics Explicit

Suggested Questions:

  • Do you have any What If . . . ? questions? (Answers will vary.)
  • How did you find the area of the water dropped circles on your paper towels? (Answers will vary.)
  • Which paper towel has the best absorbency? (Answers will vary. Some students may focus on the smallest area, saying this shows that it “soaks it up” faster. The mathematical focus is on finding the area of a circle, so using what the class decides is fine for this discussion.)
  • What does your table in the Initial Challenge tell you about circles? (Answers will vary. Leaving this as an open question will help students to look for patterns. They may not see the relationship between radius and area yet, but it will start the conversation. Some students may say the radius is half the diameter. Some students may think about a square and look at the relationship between the diameter squared and the area and say that the area is always a little less than that. Some students might square the radius and say that about 3 of those will be the area. At this time, accept all reasonable patterns they see in the table.)

Have groups share their thinking on the three strategies in What If . . . ? Situation A. As a group shares its thinking, ask these questions to the whole class:

  • Do you agree with this group’s analysis of the strategy? Why or why not? (Answers will vary. All the strategies shared in What If . . . ? Situation A are correct strategies.)
  • How does this strategy show up in our table from the Initial Challenge? (Answers will vary. Camila’s strategy is looking at the radius length, so relating her thinking to what students may have been investigating with the radius and area relationship could come up. Harlow’s and Zaire’s strategies are looking at the diameter and relationships to areas, so these could relate to what students may have discussed with diameter and area relationships in the table.)

Now What Do Students Know?

Ask students to reflect on the discussion and answer the Now What Do You Know? questions.

See answers to the problem for more information about the strategies and embedded mathematics.

Reflecting on Student Learning  

Use the following questions to assess student understanding at the end of the lesson.  

• What evidence do I have that students understand the Now What Do You Know? question?

  • Where did my students get stuck?
  • What strategies did they use?
  • What breakthroughs did my students have today?

• How will I use this to plan for tomorrow? For the next time I teach this lesson?

• Where will I have the opportunity to reinforce these ideas as I continue through this unit? The next unit?
